criterion_notes.c1: Topically addresses achieving universal access to rural and peri-urban drinking water supply and sanitation in developing regions.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper passes because it discusses sector financing governance, institutional structures, subsidies, cost sharing/cost recovery, credit mechanisms, and regulatory controls on private participation. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it also touches on rule-type mechanisms (specifically tariff/cost-recovery rules, cross-subsidies, peri-urban property rights, and microcredit loan terms in Appendix A), although mainly as high-level policy prescriptions and macro-financing strategies rather than an operational socio-legal analysis; regardless, under both readings the paper is excluded for lack of empirical evidence (E05).
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05): this is a policy strategy overview and back-of-the-envelope global costing exercise ('orders of magnitude') that multiplies secondary UN/WHO population projections by assumed 'best practice' unit costs and proposes an illustrative financing plan, with no empirical research design, no primary data analysis, and no systematic empirical synthesis (only brief descriptive policy examples such as a two-paragraph summary of Grameen Bank lending in Appendix A).
criterion_notes.c4: Models aggregate capital financial requirements (US$ billions) and normative funding shares needed to reach 1990-2000 coverage targets rather than measuring empirical household or community service access, connection, reliability, or affordability outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: No empirical study design or identifiable empirical population-exposure-outcome analysis; relies on aggregate regional projections and hypothetical financing assumptions.

evidence_quotes.quote: This article develops a model of cost and financing strategies for rural and peri-urban water supply and sanitation.
On the financing side, it suggests restructuring the financing of the sector with improved efficiency and greater cost recovery in urban services; full recovery of operation and maintenance costs;

The indicative cost figures and suggested financing plan are intended to provide the rationale and examine the scope for generating the additional resources through various means, thereby suggesting a set of actions that are needed.
Table 4 provides a suggested financing plan for the additional resources needed (ie over and above estimated current expenditure levels).

raw_response.exposure: Proposed sector financing and cost-recovery strategies (cost sharing, cost recovery, subsidies, intrasectoral budget restructuring, credit schemes, and external aid)
raw_response.outcome: Estimated aggregate capital cost requirements (US$ billions) and hypothetical annual financing targets for 1990-2000
raw_response.population_and_sample: Aggregate rural and peri-urban populations to be covered (1990-2000) in Africa, Asia, and Latin America from secondary UN/WHO/UNICEF reports (no empirical sample)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the paper topically discusses rural and peri-urban water supply and sanitation access and proposes financing and cost-recovery policies, it is a non-empirical policy overview and indicative macro-costing exercise ('orders of magnitude') multiplying secondary WHO/UN coverage targets by assumed unit costs and proposing hypothetical budget reallocations and funding shares, with no empirical research method, primary data, or systematic empirical synthesis. Both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2 yield exclusion on E05 grounds.
raw_response.study_design: Indicative macro-costing model and policy overview (non-empirical)
